key_insight: Longitudinal clinical retrieval should allocate limited evidence across time, rather than repeatedly retrieve similar passages that may miss important transitions.
clinical_relevance: For oncology record review, time-aware retrieval may help surface sparsely documented recurrences or therapy changes, but clinical accuracy remains unvalidated.
method: Separate temporal evidence allocation, candidate reconstruction, and clinical validation.
Compare Temporal-15 with Global-50 retrieval using two-stage reconstruction.
Test prompted precedence rules and explore temporal coverage under fixed evidence budgets.
evidence_signal: Across 13 queries over 20 patient records, Temporal-15 achieved milestone slot recall of 0.538 versus 0.388 for Global-50, but retrieved 496 versus 50 indexed units per query.
watch_item: Unequal evidence budgets confound the main comparison, and without expert reference timelines, the results measure retrieval behavior—not clinical accuracy.
paper_title: Temporal Evidence Allocation For Longitudinal Clinical Retrieval: A Position And Technical Report
